Part 2 continues a thought record by identifying thinking traps, examining supporting and challenging evidence, and creating a balanced alternative. The aim is a fairer thought that fits the evidence and supports effective action, not forced positivity.

## Challenging the Hot Thought {#challenging-the-hot-thought}

Ask what evidence supports the thought, what evidence does not support it, and what you might say to a close friend in the same situation.

## Balanced Alternatives {#balanced-alternatives}

Develop an alternative that acknowledges the difficulty without treating the original hot thought as the only possible interpretation.

## Thought Record Part 2 {#thought-record-part-2}

Continue from the situation, emotions, and hot thought recorded in Part 1:

### 4. Identify Thinking Traps

Check any patterns that apply, such as all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralizing, mental filtering, disqualifying the positive, mind reading, fortune telling, catastrophizing, minimizing, emotional reasoning, should statements, labelling, personalization, or overestimating threat.

### 5. Supporting Evidence

List factual evidence that supports the hot thought. Separate observable facts from assumptions and feelings.

### 6. Challenging Evidence

List facts the hot thought overlooks or contradicts. Consider past experiences, alternative explanations, and what a trusted person might notice.

### 7. Alternative Balanced Thought

Write a fair interpretation that includes all the evidence. Ask how you or a best friend could understand the situation. Rate how much you believe the new thought from 0 to 100.

### 8. Re-rate Emotion and Mood

Rate each emotion again from 0 to 100. The goal is not to force a lower number; it is to notice what changes after considering a fuller account.

#### Text Version

Just because we believe our "hot thought" does not necessarily mean it's true. You may be saying "but I feel like it's true", however, a feeling is not a fact. Feelings are not evidence for anything - they are just feelings. Indeed, feelings are real and valid, but the strength of your feelings does not prove the convictions of your thoughts. Remember, thoughts are not facts. In columns 5 and 6, we write down the evidence that supports your hot thought and evidence that does not support it. Seeking evidence is not easy to do. We often come up with a lot of

**assumptions that we think are facts. What's the difference?**

Here are some examples to think about, try to identify which ones are factual: I could tell she didn't like me by the way she looked at me She had a peculiar look on her face. She said she was tired I know he doesn't love me, if he did, he would know by now what I like He did get me what I wanted for Christmas when t gave him a list last time All teenagers are lazy My teenager does not care about how the house looks, like I do My friend does not want to be my friend anymore because she didn't text me back She did tell me that she has been very busy and stressed with a work project

##### FINDING EVIDENCE THAT DOES NOT SUPPORT THE HOT THOUGHT

Use the questions below to complete column 6 of the thought record: Have I had any experiences that show that this thought is not completely

**true all the time?**

If my best friend or someone I loved had this thought, what would I tell

**them?**

If my best friend or someone who loves me knew I was thinking this thought, what would they say to me? What evidence would they point

**out to me that would suggest that my thoughts were not 100% true?**

When I am not feeling this way, do I think about this type of situation any

**differently? How?**

When I have felt this way in the past, what did I think about that helped

**me feel better?**

Have I been in this type of situation before? What happened? Is there anything different between this situation and previous ones? What have I

**learned from prior experiences that could help me now?**

#### Text Version

Are there any small things that contradict my thoughts, which I might be

**discounting as not important?**

Five years from now, if I look back at this situation, will I look at it any

**differently? Will I focus on any different part of my experience?**

Are there any strengths or positives in me or the situation, which am

**ignoring?**

Am I jumping to any conclusions which are not completely justified by the

**evidence?**

Is there any evidence that might lead to a different conclusion than the

**one I've made?**

When examining the evidence that challenges the hot thought it is important to consider the effects of that thought on your life. Is this thought helpful to me? Will thoughts like this help me achieve my goals and a life worth living? Do thoughts like this truly have my best interests

**at heart?**

##### CREATING ALTERNATIVES OR MORE BALANCED THINKING

In working through columns 5 and 6, the evidence may now suggest that the originally held hot thought may not be entirely true. So now it is important to actually replace the original thought with an alternative thought that is more balanced and reflective of reality. This is done in column 7 of the thought record.

##### HOT THOUGHT

Nothing ever works our for me. can't stand it when people don't like me. I'm a failure. You can't trust anyone, Thevll just hurt you.

##### NEW BALANCED THOUGHT

I have had my share of things not work out, but good things have also happened in my life. Although it would feel better if everyone liked me, I can survive without everyone's approval. It is important that those people I really value, think well of me and help me grow as a person. I have failed at some things I've tried. I have been successful at many others. Not everyone can or should be trusted. Trust needs to be earned and I need to give some people a chance. Can you see how the first column is written in extremes and absolutes? The second column is a more balanced version, with an alternative way of thinking about things. The second approach takes work to create, and a great deal of insight. The change does not happen overnight. The extreme automatic thoughts have taken years to become believable, so it will take time,

#### Text Version

patience, and lots of practice to shift our thoughts. After establishing the new balanced thought, rate how much you believe in the new thought on a scale of O - 100.

##### BEST FRIEND TECHNIQUE

The Best Friend Technique is designed to help you gain some objectivity on the situation. It helps to expand your limited perspective and invite more self compassion and empathy. This technique poses some variation of the following question: "If your best friend was in this situation, what would you say to them? If you have a really wise and loving best friend, what

**would they say to you if you told them your thoughts?**

##### RE RATE YOUR EMOTIONS/MOOD

Once you have challenged and reframed the thought to a more alternative balanced thought, it is important to re rate your Emotions/Mood on a scale of 0-100 in column 8. We may not entirely buy into the new balanced thought at first but we can take notice of how we are feeling after we have gone through the process of putting our hot thought on trial. HOME PRACTICE: For this week's home practice, experiment completing an entire thought record from columns 1-8 about a situation that caused an emotional response. You can also complete the remaining sections of the thought record from last week's home practice. The next pages have two sample thought records if you need any further help.
